screens.title: Synchronous Communication: RESTful APIs
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll learn what makes an A P I truly RESTful and why that matters for scalable systems. REST is an architectural style built on a handful of constraints that, when followed, produce predictable, maintainable services that fit naturally on HTTP. You'll learn how resources are named and represented, how standard HTTP methods map to CRUD actions, and how statelessness and idempotency keep services scalable and resilient. We'll also walk through practical examples, like a product catalog and a blog platform, to see real request and response shapes. Along the way I will point out common pitfalls such as using POST for every operation or relying on server-side session state, and we'll cover how to use status codes, versioning, and pagination to build APIs your clients can rely on. By the end you'll be able to assess an A P I design against REST constraints and choose appropriate methods and responses for common operations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives will guide your practice with RESTful design. First, you will be able to state REST's core principles and explain why resource orientation matters; that helps you model endpoints that match client mental models. Second, you'll correctly choose HTTP methods and understand idempotency, safety, and when to use PATCH versus PUT; this reduces accidental side effects in production. Third, you'll design request and response shapes, pick status codes, and use headers for caching and content negotiation; that improves client interoperability. And fourth, you'll recognize common pitfalls—using POST as an RPC, storing session state on the server, or exposing secrets in URIs—and apply best practices such as HTTPS, versioning, and rate limiting. Each objective connects a concrete skill to a real system benefit so you can measure competency as you design or review APIs.

screens.title: What is REST?
screens.narratorSegment: REST is an architectural style, not a protocol. That means it defines constraints you can apply to an HTTP-based system to achieve desirable properties like scalability and simplicity. The most important idea is resource orientation: anything you can name can be treated as a resource and identified by a URI. A resource's state is transferred as a representation—commonly JSON in modern web APIs. REST also relies on a uniform interface so clients and servers have consistent expectations about verbs and resource manipulation. A concrete example is a product catalog service where /products lists items and /products/P123 identifies a single product. A common misconception is to equate REST with any HTTP A P I. Many APIs call themselves RESTful while violating constraints like statelessness or the uniform interface; that reduces the benefits REST provides. Key takeaways: treat entities as resources with clear URIs, exchange representations to manipulate state, and use the uniform interface to keep clients simple and interoperable. Reflect: which aspects of your existing APIs already match resource-oriented thinking, and where do they diverge? What is REST? means rest organizes systems around named resources and a consistent set of operations for manipulating their representations.. In practical terms, an architectural style based on resources and a uniform interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What is REST?
Definition

Resource-oriented architecture

Resources are identified by URIs like /products or /posts/{id}. Representations such as JSON convey resource state between client and server.

Representation example: JSON body for a product
{
  "id": "P123",
  "name": "Widget",
  "price": 29.99
}
Analogy

Think of resources as named records in a catalog. URIs are stable labels and representations are the printed pages clients read or modify.

Concrete Example
GET /products returns a list. GET /products/P123 returns details for product P123.
Common Misconception
Calling an HTTP API RESTful while ignoring statelessness or the uniform interface weakens its benefits.
Key Takeaway

REST is about modeling resources and using a consistent interface so clients and servers interoperate predictably.

screens.title: REST Constraints Overview
screens.narratorSegment: REST is defined by a set of constraints that steer system behavior. Client-Server separation gives each side a clear role: the client focuses on user experience while the server manages data and business logic; this keeps concerns separated and allows independent evolution. Statelessness requires each request to contain all context necessary to process it, which improves horizontal scalability and simplifies recovery. Cacheable responses let clients and intermediaries avoid unnecessary load by declaring how responses can be reused. The uniform interface bundles four ideas: consistent resource identification via URIs, manipulation through representations, self-descriptive messages with standard headers and content types, and an optional HATEOAS model where resources include links to related actions. HATEOAS is often omitted in practice because it adds complexity, but it remains part of the ideal REST constraint set. A typical misconception is to implement some constraints while ignoring others; the benefits scale with how many constraints you apply. Think about which constraints your systems already obey and which ones you can adopt to improve clarity and scalability. REST Constraints Overview means apply rest constraints progressively: each one brings clarity and operational benefits; uniform interface is the most impactful.. In practical terms, client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, and hateoas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › REST Constraints
Core constraints and why they matter
  • Client-Server: separate UI from data and logic for independent scaling.
  • Stateless: each request contains all needed info so any server can handle it.
  • Cacheable: responses should declare freshness to reduce load.
  • Uniform interface: consistent URIs, representations, and methods.
  • HATEOAS: resources link to valid next actions; useful but often omitted.
Practical note: systems get more predictable the more constraints you follow; start with statelessness and uniform interfaces.
Quick checks
Does each URI name a resource?
Does each request include required context?
Are responses explicitly cacheable or not?
Key Takeaway

Start by enforcing stateless requests and a clear uniform interface; other constraints enhance scalability and clarity.

screens.title: HTTP Methods and CRUD
screens.narratorSegment: HTTP methods provide a uniform interface to manipulate resources and directly map to CRUD operations. GET retrieves resources and should be safe and idempotent, meaning it does not change server state and multiple identical requests result in the same effect. POST creates new resources and is usually not idempotent; sending the same creation twice may create two records. PUT replaces a resource or creates it if missing and is idempotent because applying the same representation repeatedly yields the same outcome. PATCH applies a partial update and can be designed to be idempotent, but you must craft the semantics carefully. DELETE removes a resource and is idempotent: deleting something repeatedly yields the same final state. A frequent developer mistake is to use POST for all actions, turning the A P I into an RPC surface that loses caching and semantic clarity. When in doubt, model your resource and ask: is this a creation, a read, a full replace, a partial update, or a deletion? That decision guides the correct HTTP method. HTTP Methods and CRUD means use methods to express intent: get for reads, post for create, put for replace, patch for partial updates, delete for removals.. In practical terms, mapping get, post, put, patch, delete to resource operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › HTTP Methods
Method → CRUD
GET
Safe, idempotent — read resources
POST
Create — typically not idempotent
PUT
Replace or create — idempotent
PATCH
Partial update — design for idempotency if needed
DELETE
Remove resource — idempotent
Concrete example
Product catalog: GET /products, GET /products/P123, POST /products to add, PUT /products/P123 to replace, PATCH /products/P123 to change a price, DELETE /products/P123 to remove.
Mistake to avoid: using POST /updatePrice or POST /updateUserStatus rather than PATCH /users/{id} with a partial update payload.

screens.title: GET: Read operations and safety
screens.narratorSegment: GET is the primary read method and has two important qualities: safety and idempotency. Safety means a GET should not alter server state. Idempotency means repeated identical GETs produce the same observable effect and response. These guarantees allow caching and retry strategies to be safe. For example, a client retrieving a product list with GET /products can rely on caches and intermediaries to serve that content when appropriate. A small curl example shows a typical GET request and a 200 response containing JSON. Remember to set content type headers and consider Cache-Control directives so intermediaries know how to treat the response. A common misconception is expecting GET to always return identical bytes; servers may return different timestamps or pagination links. The key is that GET does not change the server state. Takeaway: model reads with GET, use explicit caching headers, and avoid side effects in GET handlers so clients and CDNs can optimize delivery. GET: Read operations and safety means get should be safe and idempotent; use caching headers to improve performance and avoid side effects during reads.. In practical terms, use get for safe, idempotent reads and enable caching. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › GET: Read
Curl example and response
curl -i -H "Accept: application/json" https://api.example.com/products

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: max-age=60

[
  { "id": "P123", "name": "Widget", "price": 29.99 },
  { "id": "P124", "name": "Gadget", "price": 19.99 }
]
Set Cache-Control and Content-Type to help intermediaries and clients. Avoid performing writes in GET handlers so caches remain safe to use.
Example scenario
A storefront fetches /products on page load. If responses include Cache-Control, CDNs can serve cached lists and reduce load on the origin service.
Key Takeaway

Model reads as GET, return explicit cache headers, and keep handlers side-effect free.

screens.title: POST: Creating resources
screens.narratorSegment: POST is the usual choice to create new resources under a collection URI. It is generally not idempotent because submitting the same POST payload twice may create two resources. When a POST succeeds, the server should return 201 Created and include the Location header pointing to the new resource's URI. For example, POST /products with a JSON body describing a product can produce a response that includes the newly created product's ID. A common developer error is using POST for updates instead of partial updates with PATCH or full replaces with PUT; that obscures intent and prevents intermediaries from optimizing behavior. Security-wise, POST bodies should be sent over HTTPS and not include sensitive identifiers in the URI. When building APIs, document whether POST operations are idempotent in special cases and provide guidance on safe retries. POST: Creating resources means use post for creating resources; return 201 created and location. avoid using post as a catch-all rpc method.. In practical terms, use post to create new resources and return 201 created. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › POST: Create
Curl create example
curl -i -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "name": "New Product", "price": 39.99 }' \
  https://api.example.com/products

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: https://api.example.com/products/P789
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": "P789", "name": "New Product", "price": 39.99 }
Include Location for created resource. Document retry semantics because POST is usually not safe to retry blindly.
Scenario
A client submits a product form to POST /products. The server validates and returns 201 with the new resource link.
Best practice: return a consistent response body and Location header so clients can follow up with GET if needed.

screens.title: PUT vs PATCH
screens.narratorSegment: PUT and PATCH both update a resource but express different semantics. PUT is intended for full replacement: the client sends the complete representation, and the server stores that state. PUT is idempotent because replacing with the same representation yields the same state. PATCH expresses partial updates; the request contains only the fields to change. PATCH can be idempotent if designed carefully—for example, carrying a set operation that makes the same change when applied multiple times—but it's not inherently idempotent. Consider an e-commerce example: updating all details for product P123 is a PUT /products/P123 with the full JSON, while adjusting only the price is PATCH /products/P123 with { "price": 29.99 }. A common mistake is mixing semantics or allowing PUT to behave like a merge. If you choose PUT for replace, ensure your implementation overwrites missing fields or clearly documents merge behavior. Clear documentation prevents client-server mismatches and surprising behavior. PUT vs PATCH means use put for full replaces and patch for partial updates; document semantics to avoid subtle bugs and mismatches.. In practical terms, full replace or partial update — choose semantics deliberately. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › PUT vs PATCH
PUT (full replace)
PUT /products/P123
{
  "id": "P123",
  "name": "Updated Name",
  "price": 24.99,
  "inventory": 10
}
Idempotent: sending the same full body repeatedly keeps the resource state identical.
PATCH (partial update)
PATCH /products/P123
{ "price": 29.99 }
Partial: change only the fields you need. Design to avoid non-idempotent operations like increments unless documented.
Key Takeaway

Be explicit: PUT replaces, PATCH modifies. Document behavior so clients can write safe retries and updates.

screens.title: DELETE and Idempotency
screens.narratorSegment: DELETE removes a resource and is idempotent: issuing DELETE multiple times results in the same end state — the resource is absent. The server should respond with an appropriate status code, such as 204 No Content when deletion succeeds and there's no body, or 404 Not Found if the resource does not exist. Idempotency here helps clients retry safely when a network failure occurs. A common mistake is leaving soft-delete semantics undocumented; if your DELETE performs a soft delete, document the behavior and whether the resource URI becomes valid again. From a security perspective, ensure only authorized clients can delete resources and return 401 or 403 as applicable. Example: DELETE /products/P123 removes product P123; subsequent DELETEs should be tolerated and return an appropriate status. Question to reflect on: if your system uses soft deletes, how will clients discover whether a resource is recoverable or permanently gone? DELETE and Idempotency means delete should be idempotent; return clear status codes and document whether deletes are hard or soft to avoid client confusion.. In practical terms, deleting resources and idempotent semantics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. narration.text: DELETE removes a resource and is idempotent: issuing DELETE multiple times results in the same end state — the resource is absent. screens.narratorSegment: Status codes communicate the outcome of a request in a standardized way so clients can act without parsing response bodies. 2xx codes indicate success: 200 OK for a successful retrieval, 201 Created when a new resource is made, and 204 No Content when an operation succeeds with no body. 3xx codes indicate redirection; 301 signals permanent moves. 4xx codes are client errors: 400 Bad Request for malformed payloads, 401 Unauthorized when authentication is missing or invalid, 403 Forbidden when authorization fails, 404 Not Found for missing resources, and 409 Conflict when a request violates current server state. 5xx codes signal server errors such as 500 Internal Server Error or 503 Service Unavailable. A common mistake is returning 200 for every response and putting error details in the body; this breaks client behaviors and intermediaries. Use appropriate codes and pair them with consistent error response structures so clients can distinguish transient from permanent failures and implement retries or user messages correctly. screens.title: Statelessness and Scalability
screens.narratorSegment: Statelessness is central to REST: servers must not store client context between requests. Each request carries its own authentication, parameters, and state necessary for processing. This constraint enables simple load balancing because any server instance can handle any request without sticky sessions. For example, a client includes an authorization token and request parameters each time it calls GET /products or PATCH /products/P123. If your system relies on server-side sessions to track user state, horizontal scaling becomes harder and failover more complex. A common trade-off is to use tokens like JWTs so the client supplies verifiable claims each request; however, JWTs require rotation and careful security practices. Another operational note is to put ephemeral caches closer to clients and keep the origin stateless so you can scale by adding instances. Reflect on your architecture: can any request be handled by a different server without losing correctness? If not, identify the state being kept and consider moving it into the request or a shared data store. Statelessness and Scalability means design requests so any server can process them independently; this simplifies load balancing and horizontal scaling.. In practical terms, why each request must carry its own context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll learn what makes an A P I truly RESTful and why that matters for scalable systems. REST is an architectural style built on a handful of constraints that, when followed, produce predictable, maintainable services that fit naturally on HTTP. You'll learn how resources are named and represented, how standard HTTP methods map to CRUD actions, and how statelessness and idempotency keep services scalable and resilient. We'll also walk through practical examples, like a product catalog and a blog platform, to see real request and response shapes. Along the way I will point out common pitfalls such as using POST for every operation or relying on server-side session state, and we'll cover how to use status codes, versioning, and pagination to build APIs your clients can rely on. By the end you'll be able to assess an A P I design against REST constraints and choose appropriate methods and responses for common operations.

These objectives will guide your practice with RESTful design. First, you will be able to state REST's core principles and explain why resource orientation matters; that helps you model endpoints that match client mental models. Second, you'll correctly choose HTTP methods and understand idempotency, safety, and when to use PATCH versus PUT; this reduces accidental side effects in production. Third, you'll design request and response shapes, pick status codes, and use headers for caching and content negotiation; that improves client interoperability. And fourth, you'll recognize common pitfalls—using POST as an RPC, storing session state on the server, or exposing secrets in URIs—and apply best practices such as HTTPS, versioning, and rate limiting. Each objective connects a concrete skill to a real system benefit so you can measure competency as you design or review APIs.

These additional objectives focus on real design tasks and avoiding common mistakes. You will learn to design and consume RESTful endpoints with appropriate request and response bodies and headers so clients can implement integrations without guesswork. You'll practice mapping CRUD to HTTP verbs in realistic scenarios such as product catalogs and blog platforms, and you'll learn to apply pagination and versioning patterns where needed. Finally, we'll identify anti-patterns like treating the A P I as an RPC layer and hiding state on the server, and we'll cover security basics like avoiding sensitive data in URIs and enforcing HTTPS. Each objective is tied to a measurable design practice so you can validate that your APIs are both correct and maintainable. Learning Objectives (continued) means translate rest principles into concrete endpoints, request/response shapes, and safe operational practices.. In practical terms, practical design and common pitfalls. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

REST is an architectural style, not a protocol. That means it defines constraints you can apply to an HTTP-based system to achieve desirable properties like scalability and simplicity. The most important idea is resource orientation: anything you can name can be treated as a resource and identified by a URI. A resource's state is transferred as a representation—commonly JSON in modern web APIs. REST also relies on a uniform interface so clients and servers have consistent expectations about verbs and resource manipulation. A concrete example is a product catalog service where /products lists items and /products/P123 identifies a single product. A common misconception is to equate REST with any HTTP A P I. Many APIs call themselves RESTful while violating constraints like statelessness or the uniform interface; that reduces the benefits REST provides. Key takeaways: treat entities as resources with clear URIs, exchange representations to manipulate state, and use the uniform interface to keep clients simple and interoperable. Reflect: which aspects of your existing APIs already match resource-oriented thinking, and where do they diverge? What is REST? means rest organizes systems around named resources and a consistent set of operations for manipulating their representations.. In practical terms, an architectural style based on resources and a uniform interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

REST is defined by a set of constraints that steer system behavior. Client-Server separation gives each side a clear role: the client focuses on user experience while the server manages data and business logic; this keeps concerns separated and allows independent evolution. Statelessness requires each request to contain all context necessary to process it, which improves horizontal scalability and simplifies recovery. Cacheable responses let clients and intermediaries avoid unnecessary load by declaring how responses can be reused. The uniform interface bundles four ideas: consistent resource identification via URIs, manipulation through representations, self-descriptive messages with standard headers and content types, and an optional HATEOAS model where resources include links to related actions. HATEOAS is often omitted in practice because it adds complexity, but it remains part of the ideal REST constraint set. A typical misconception is to implement some constraints while ignoring others; the benefits scale with how many constraints you apply. Think about which constraints your systems already obey and which ones you can adopt to improve clarity and scalability. REST Constraints Overview means apply rest constraints progressively: each one brings clarity and operational benefits; uniform interface is the most impactful.. In practical terms, client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, and hateoas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

HTTP methods provide a uniform interface to manipulate resources and directly map to CRUD operations. GET retrieves resources and should be safe and idempotent, meaning it does not change server state and multiple identical requests result in the same effect. POST creates new resources and is usually not idempotent; sending the same creation twice may create two records. PUT replaces a resource or creates it if missing and is idempotent because applying the same representation repeatedly yields the same outcome. PATCH applies a partial update and can be designed to be idempotent, but you must craft the semantics carefully. DELETE removes a resource and is idempotent: deleting something repeatedly yields the same final state. A frequent developer mistake is to use POST for all actions, turning the A P I into an RPC surface that loses caching and semantic clarity. When in doubt, model your resource and ask: is this a creation, a read, a full replace, a partial update, or a deletion? That decision guides the correct HTTP method. HTTP Methods and CRUD means use methods to express intent: get for reads, post for create, put for replace, patch for partial updates, delete for removals.. In practical terms, mapping get, post, put, patch, delete to resource operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

GET is the primary read method and has two important qualities: safety and idempotency. Safety means a GET should not alter server state. Idempotency means repeated identical GETs produce the same observable effect and response. These guarantees allow caching and retry strategies to be safe. For example, a client retrieving a product list with GET /products can rely on caches and intermediaries to serve that content when appropriate. A small curl example shows a typical GET request and a 200 response containing JSON. Remember to set content type headers and consider Cache-Control directives so intermediaries know how to treat the response. A common misconception is expecting GET to always return identical bytes; servers may return different timestamps or pagination links. The key is that GET does not change the server state. Takeaway: model reads with GET, use explicit caching headers, and avoid side effects in GET handlers so clients and CDNs can optimize delivery. GET: Read operations and safety means get should be safe and idempotent; use caching headers to improve performance and avoid side effects during reads.. In practical terms, use get for safe, idempotent reads and enable caching. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

POST is the usual choice to create new resources under a collection URI. It is generally not idempotent because submitting the same POST payload twice may create two resources. When a POST succeeds, the server should return 201 Created and include the Location header pointing to the new resource's URI. For example, POST /products with a JSON body describing a product can produce a response that includes the newly created product's ID. A common developer error is using POST for updates instead of partial updates with PATCH or full replaces with PUT; that obscures intent and prevents intermediaries from optimizing behavior. Security-wise, POST bodies should be sent over HTTPS and not include sensitive identifiers in the URI. When building APIs, document whether POST operations are idempotent in special cases and provide guidance on safe retries. PUT and PATCH both update a resource but express different semantics. PUT is intended for full replacement: the client sends the complete representation, and the server stores that state. PUT is idempotent because replacing with the same representation yields the same state. PATCH expresses partial updates; the request contains only the fields to change. PATCH can be idempotent if designed carefully—for example, carrying a set operation that makes the same change when applied multiple times—but it's not inherently idempotent. Consider an e-commerce example: updating all details for product P123 is a PUT /products/P123 with the full JSON, while adjusting only the price is PATCH /products/P123 with { "price": 29.99 }. A common mistake is mixing semantics or allowing PUT to behave like a merge. If you choose PUT for replace, ensure your implementation overwrites missing fields or clearly documents merge behavior. Clear documentation prevents client-server mismatches and surprising behavior. PUT vs PATCH means use put for full replaces and patch for partial updates; document semantics to avoid subtle bugs and mismatches.. In practical terms, full replace or partial update — choose semantics deliberately. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Statelessness is central to REST: servers must not store client context between requests. Each request carries its own authentication, parameters, and state necessary for processing. This constraint enables simple load balancing because any server instance can handle any request without sticky sessions. For example, a client includes an authorization token and request parameters each time it calls GET /products or PATCH /products/P123. If your system relies on server-side sessions to track user state, horizontal scaling becomes harder and failover more complex. A common trade-off is to use tokens like JWTs so the client supplies verifiable claims each request; however, JWTs require rotation and careful security practices. Another operational note is to put ephemeral caches closer to clients and keep the origin stateless so you can scale by adding instances. Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, REST treats data and actions as resources identified by URIs; representations like JSON convey resource state. Second, HTTP methods express intent: GET for reads, POST for create, PUT for replace, PATCH for partial update, and DELETE for removal; choosing the correct verb improves client behavior and caching. Third, statelessness and idempotency are operational constraints that support scalability and safe retries. Fourth, use status codes and consistent error formats to signal outcomes reliably. Fifth, follow practical patterns such as versioning, pagination, and secure transport to keep APIs maintainable and safe. Finally, avoid common mistakes like using POST as an RPC catch-all or storing session state server-side.
